title: I Make, Phyllis, in My Soul, While Absent
text:
I make, Phyllis, in my soul, while absent,

spirited preparations to speak to you,

and you with one glance undo them;

I fall silent, troubled and obedient.


But my confusion is so eloquent

(effect of these faithful disturbances),

that the voice which fled my arguments

persuades in the eyes and on the brow.


It is clear that if you feel yourself soften

so as to put my truth in doubt,

you have neither license nor right left.


For this love strips them of ornament;

for introducing pity, Phyllis, into your breast

cannot be the jurisdiction of art.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the conceit that silence and confusion persuade better than prepared speech.

title: On an Ancient Palm at Supreme Height
text:
On an ancient palm at supreme height,

with the sacred odors of the East,

for its birth and death together,

the phoenix makes nest and sepulcher.


It moves its wings to burn securely,

for the fire is obedient to its hope;

and so, its faithful flames more brightly

restore it to the future age.


In this way, in the sacred palm

of our high courage, my cheerful thought

presumes to burn among its branches;


for your ardor gives life to what it consumes;

and so the one who to its flames entrusts

the great deposit of the soul is not rash.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the phoenix conceit of fire that consumes and restores the soul.

title: Whether You Curl or Let Down the Natural Gold
text:
Whether you curl or let down the natural gold,

or aspire with industry to arrange it,

whether you see its loops or waves shine

when, free, you commend it to your ladies;


or whether, by a new law of love, you fasten it

among rich diamonds and sapphires,

or withdraw it beneath beautiful plumes,

and pretend to counterfeit a manly dress;


Adonis seeks you before his Venus,

the goddess already holds you for her Adonis,

and your hair deceives them both;


but I, in the same miraculous doubt,

while both lovers are found in you,

die for both, and from jealousy of them.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the androgynous Adonis/Venus conceit centered on the beloved's hair.

title: Tell Me, Common Father, Since You Are Just...
text:
"Tell me, common Father, since you are just,

why must your providence allow

that innocence, dragging chains,

while fraud rises to an august tribunal?


"Who gives strength to the sturdy arm

that makes firm resistance to your laws,

and makes zeal, which reveres them most,

groan at the feet of the unjust victor?


"We see wicked hands wave victorious palms,

virtue groaning

at triumph in unjust rejoicing."


This I was saying, when, laughing,

a celestial nymph appeared and told me:

"Blind man! Is earth the center of souls?"
editorial_note: The translation keeps the complaint against injustice and the celestial rebuke that widens the scale beyond earth.

title: Who Will Give Me Jasmines and Violets...
text:
Who will give me jasmines and violets

to gird the temples of a victor,

who turned disdain into caresses

where love blunted so many arrows?


Goddess Occasion, do you produce or subject

the fatal beginning of our goods?

You subdued Clori; you have omnipotence,

and the planets are your ministers.


You subdued me by sudden assault

(with fraud traced by love itself),

the force in which it enclosed all its glory;


for he was born of theft and treachery pleases him.

I came, I saw, and I won a greater victory

than the East gave to a Latin victor.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the mock-triumphal language and the goddess Occasion's ambush.

title: Of the Union, Silvio, by Which Love Prospers
text:
Of the union, Silvio, by which love prospers

or deifies our souls, the concept

that hope forms is so perfect

that it lightens the oppression of the yoke.


And so, whoever loves and says he does not hope,

to display more faith to the beloved object,

loses respect for his inner truth,

without whose relief he could not even breathe.


Though yes, generous in delay

(while it is not turned into glory),

it invites him to nobler refinements.


Let him suffer and hope, but with so strong a law

that even if strength fails him, he never asks

suffering for hope.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the sonnet's argument that love's suffering must still preserve hope.

title: Look at Me with Pity; and Let the Comet Burn
text:
Look at me with pity; and let the comet burn,

Phyllis, which now looks on us pale;

for one to whom your eyes show love without wrath,

what fatal boundary does not respect him?


And absorbed (which is more) in the secret

happiness that such favor inspires in him,

he neither marvels at a higher threat,

nor interprets it in doubtful prodigies.


From these blessings, lift me to the second;

for I do not aspire to the first, though it free me

from the high indignation the portent arms.


Let its inauspicious light flash against scepters,

and as long as it leaves my rapture in peace,

let it pour discord and disorder the world.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the lover's indifference to cosmic omen as long as Phyllis grants pity.

title: Weaknesses
text:
You had none,

I only one,

that I loved.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the poem's miniature balance of blame and confession.

title: As It Was II
text:
Your sorrows were my sorrows,

mine, yours.

If you were not content,

I was not either.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the compact reciprocity of shared unhappiness.

title: The Cut Rope
text:
The cut rope can be knotted again,

it holds once more, but

it is cut.


Perhaps we will stumble upon each other again, but there

where you abandoned me you will

not find me again.
editorial_note: The translation keeps Brecht's plain image of repair that cannot undo the cut.
